Hello Marrowvale Couriers accounts team,

We have received a request to change your bank details for invoice MVC-1047. Please confirm whether this request came from you.

Please confirm by phone on the number we already have for you, or by replying from your usual address. We will not act on this request until we hear back from you.

Thank you,
Ashgrove Bakery

risk_assessment.rationale: The audio asks the recipient to stop paying invoice 1047 to the old account and instead use new bank details. This is the classic bank-detail-change invoice fraud pattern, so it should be treated as likely fraud and verified independently before any payment.

signals.explanation: Sender says the supplier has changed banks and instructs not to pay the old account, a direct attempt to divert payment.
Sender supplies a new sort code and account number and tells the recipient to make the change before paying.
signals.quote: Please make the change before you pay.

signals.explanation: Sender provides replacement payment details for invoice 1047, requesting an unusual change to how payment is made.

skeptic.argument: This is presented as a routine vendor bank-change notice from Sam Pryor at Marrowvale Couriers, quoting specific invoice 1047 and full new sort code and account number, and inviting a callback for clarification rather than demanding secrecy or immediate payment. Nothing in the transcript impersonates Ashgrove executive Dana Whitlock or pressures Ashgrove to bypass normal approval, and a legitimate supplier changing banks mid-month is a plausible explanation. Without a record contradicting Marrowvale as a supplier or its new account, the benign explanation remains possible.
skeptic.evidence_that_would_change_my_mind: Call Marrowvale Couriers on a phone number already in Ashgrove's vendor records (not 01632960735 from the recording) and confirm Sam Pryor, invoice 1047, and the new sort code 30-94-12 / account 55018273; if they deny it, I would switch to likely_fraud.
